extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; general readers and students of physical anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: A nineteenth-century anthropological overview describing the physical and physiological characters used to distinguish human races (stature, limb proportions, skull form, brain size, facial features, complexion, constitution, temperament) and the measurement/recording methods for those traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stature (average height)
rubrics_metrics.description: In comparing races as to their stature, we concern ourselves not with the tallest or shortest men of each tribe, but with the ordinary or average-sized men who may be taken as fair representatives of their whole tribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use average/mean representatives rather than extremes. Examples: Patagonians often near six feet four inches (mean ~5'11"), Bushmen average ~4'6". Note that women may be taken as about one sixteenth less than men. Compare populations co-located in same district to highlight differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions of limbs and body (limb-lengths, chest, waist, hips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology finds race-differences in proportions of limbs, and the proportions of the body (e.g., chest circumference, arm and leg lengths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish inherited differences from those produced by early training or habit of life (e.g., chest measure depends on lifestyle; soldiers and sailors differ). Examples: African negro notable for long arms and legs; Aymara Indian notable for shortness. Use limb proportions (e.g., fingertip-to-knee) to compare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformation of the skull (cephalic index / breadth-to-length)
rubrics_metrics.description: When looked at from the vertical or top view, the proportion of breadth to length (cephalic index) distinguishes skull-types: dolichocephalic (long-headed), mesocephalic (middle-headed), brachycephalic (short-headed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure cross diameter relative to front-back diameter (examples given: negro index ~70, European ~80, Samoyed ~85). Consider top, front, and back views for width-to-height ratios. Note that skull shape can be altered by pressure (models could be reshaped), so interpret with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial profile and prognathism (facial angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Profile view shows differences in facial angle: some peoples are prognathous (forward-jawed) while others are orthognathous (upright-jawed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use side profiles to assess facial angle; examples: Australian and African shown as prognathous, European as orthognathous. Combine upper and lower profile features to understand overall face slope (e.g., 'ape-like' slope vs upright).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain capacity and convolution complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of brain is usually ascertained by measuring skull capacity (filling skulls with shot or seed). Professor Flower's mean estimates: Australian ~79 cu. in.; African ~85 cu. in.; European ~91 cu. in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record skull capacities with standard methods (shot/seed). Anatomists also compare complexity of brain convolutions; a more full and intricate system of brain-cells and fibers is argued to relate to higher intellectual power, though observations are acknowledged as far from perfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters of facial features (nose, lips, eyelids, cheekbones, chin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctive soft-part features — nose shape, lips, cheeks, chin, eyelid form — provide excellent marks for distinguishing races and often reflect underlying skull shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare characteristic contrasts (e.g., aquiline Persian nose vs snub negro nose; skew-eyelids in Mongolian race; high cheek-bones). Use well-chosen photographs or portraits of representative, moderately handsome individuals for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin color (complexion) and its variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Skin color ranges from fair Northern European complexions through Mediterranean browns, Malays yellowish, American tribes brown, Australians deep-brown, to negro black-brown; the dark hue of the negro is deep brown rather than true black and changes after birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record color carefully, using Broca's set of pattern-colors for traveler observations to obtain accurate matches. Recognize that complexion varies gradually rather than in hard lines; note that sole and palm coloring, and developmental changes in infancy, are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peculiarities of constitution (skin secretions, smell, disease liability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaporation from the human skin is accompanied by a smell which differs in different races; this peculiarity indicates differences in skin secretions and appears connected with liability to certain fevers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider physiological/constitutional traits (odor, secretion patterns) as race-characters of importance for health and disease susceptibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental and moral temperament (as related to physical traits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology notes differences in mental and moral temperament among races and discusses their relation to physical characteristics like brain size and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat links between brain measures and intellectual/cultural advancement cautiously: while higher brain capacity and more complex convolutions are presented as connected to higher intellectual power, the text admits observations are imperfect and such inferences are tentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological cautions and measurement practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Care must be taken not to confuse real race-differences with alterations made by the individual's early training or habit of life; use standardized recording and measurement techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer averages over extremes; use Broca's pattern-colors for complexion; measure skull capacity with shot/seed; be aware that skull models may be physically deformed by pressure (experimental caveat); use photographs and comparative examples to illustrate distinctions.
